verses.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel.
David said to Joab and to the princes of the people, “Go, count Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring me word, that I may know how many there are.”

Joab said, “May Yahweh make his people a hundred times as many as they are. But, my lord the king, aren’t they all my lord’s servants? Why does my lord require this thing? Why will he be a cause of guilt to Israel?”
Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Therefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, then came to Jerusalem.

Joab gave up the sum of the census of the people to David. All those of Israel were one million one hundred thousand men who drew a sword; and in Judah were four hundred seventy thousand men who drew a sword.
But he didn’t count Levi and Benjamin among them; for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.
God was displeased with this thing; therefore he struck Israel.
David said to God, “I have sinned greatly, in that I have done this thing. But now put away, I beg you, the iniquity of your servant; for I have done very foolishly.”
Yahweh spoke to Gad, David’s seer, saying,
“Go and speak to David, saying, ‘Yahweh says, “I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.”’”
So Gad came to David, and said to him, “Yahweh says, ‘Take your choice:

either three years of famine; or three months to be consumed before your foes, while the sword of your enemies overtakes you; or else three days the sword of Yahweh, even pestilence in the land, and Yahweh’s angel destroying throughout all the borders of Israel. Now therefore consider what answer I shall return to him who sent me.’”
David said to Gad, “I am in distress. Let me fall, I pray, into Yahweh’s hand; for his mercies are very great. Don’t let me fall into man’s hand.”
So Yahweh sent a pestilence on Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell.

God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it. As he was about to destroy, Yahweh saw, and he relented of the disaster, and said to the destroying angel, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” Yahweh’s angel was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

David lifted up his eyes, and saw Yahweh’s angel standing between earth and the sky, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces.

David said to God, “Isn’t it I who commanded the people to be counted? It is even I who have sinned and done very wickedly; but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O Yahweh my God, be against me, and against my father’s house; but not against your people, that they should be plagued.”
Then Yahweh’s angel commanded Gad to tell David that David should go up and raise an altar to Yahweh on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spoke in Yahweh’s name.
Ornan turned back, and saw the angel; and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat.
As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshing floor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground.

Then David said to Ornan, “Give me the place of this threshing floor, that I may build an altar to Yahweh on it. You shall sell it to me for the full price, that the plague may be stopped from afflicting the people.”

Ornan said to David, “Take it for yourself, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes. Behold, I give the oxen for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meal offering. I give it all.”
King David said to Ornan, “No; but I will most certainly buy it for the full price. For I will not take that which is yours for Yahweh, nor offer a burnt offering that costs me nothing.”
So David gave to Ornan six hundred shekels  of gold by weight for the place.
David built an altar to Yahweh there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called on Yahweh; and he answered him from the sky by fire on the altar of burnt offering.
Then Yahweh commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.
At that time, when David saw that Yahweh had answered him in the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there.
For Yahweh’s tabernacle, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering, were at that time in the high place at Gibeon.
But David couldn’t go before it to inquire of God; for he was afraid because of the sword of Yahweh’s angel.

footnotes.content: Satan's breath is always near a king's pride. David forgot that his strength lay not in numbers but in God—and in that single forgetting, the Enemy found his opening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a ruler commands a numbering, he is counting his own power. David's order to count Israel was the outer shape of an inner turning away—measuring trust by soldiers instead of by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab saw plainly what the king could not: that such a numbering would bring guilt on the people. His warning—'Why will he be a cause of guilt to Israel?'—named the very sin before it fully ripened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's word prevails; Joab obeys though his heart forbids it. Obedience to a command we know to be wrong cuts deep—and sometimes we must bear the weight of another's choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One million one hundred thousand men of war—David now held the number he craved. Yet a census of strength is an unquiet comfort; it counts today's men but not tomorrow's will of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levi and Benjamin were omitted—perhaps the only fragment of Joab's resistance that remained. Even in rebellion, some ancient boundaries held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's displeasure is swift and clear. When we turn from trust to our own reckoning, He does not look away—He strikes, to call us back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's repentance came as soon as the blow fell. 'I have done very foolishly'—not the clever king speaking now, but a man who sees his own heart at last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad, the seer, steps forward as God's messenger—a name meaning 'fortune' or 'good timing,' yet he brings the Lord's word of judgment. Sometimes He sends His word through those whose names seem to promise ease.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three choices offered: famine, defeat, or plague. In each, David will lose—soldiers or food or lives. The Lord gives him the weight of choosing which sorrow will be his.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad came before David, laying out the three paths plainly. A faithful messenger brings hard truth without softening it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three terrible years, or three months of war, or three days of the angel's pestilence—all exacting their toll. David was asked to taste which judgment his sin deserved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In his distress, David chose to fall into God's hand rather than man's. 'His mercies are very great'—even in judgment, the king saw the Lord's character as the greater safety.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy thousand fell to the pestilence—a harvest of death that David's pride had sown. The price of his counting was paid in bodies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel hovered over Jerusalem with sword drawn, ready to finish the work—until the Lord saw and said, 'It is enough.' Mercy does not erase the rod, but it stays the final blow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David saw the angel between earth and heaven, the sword outstretched. The vision was terrible and plain—the Lord's judgment made visible, the sword of His justice made real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David pled that the blow fall on him alone, not his people. A true shepherd will offer his own neck rather than see the flock harmed—and the Lord hears such intercession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel commanded Gad to tell David to build an altar at the threshing floor of Ornan. Out of judgment came direction; from the place of stopping came the place to begin again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David obeyed at once, asking no second word—he had learned to listen. Obedience spoken in the Lord's name carries its own certainty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ornan turned and saw the angel while his sons hid in fear. The threshing floor, a place of common work, became a place where heaven touched earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Ornan saw David coming, he rose and bowed. The king, now humbled, walked toward this ordinary place and this ordinary man—where the Lord would meet him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asked to buy the threshing floor, that the plague might be stopped. His request was not for himself—it was an intercession, a purchase of mercy for his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ornan offered all freely—oxen, instruments, wheat. His generosity was a small echo of the Lord's: when the Lord draws near, His people often cannot help but give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David refused the gift. 'I will not offer a burnt offering that costs me nothing'—the king named the very heart of true worship: that it must cost us something real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred shekels of gold—David paid in full for the place. The price was steep, but he paid it without counting the cost twice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David built the altar and called on the Lord, and fire fell from heaven to consume the offering. The Lord answered—His anger was appeased, and David knew it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord commanded the angel to sheath his sword. Judgment ended; the reprieve had come. The blade was drawn, and now it rested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David saw that the Lord had answered at that place and sacrificed there continually. He had found the place where heaven answered earth—and it would become holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tabernacle and altar of the wilderness lay at Gibeon, high and distant. But on Ornan's threshing floor—a humble place—David discovered where the Lord would meet his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: we, too, sometimes fear the Lord's hand when we have strayed. Yet that very fear—that we cannot approach Him when our hearts are wrong—is the mercy that draws us back to Him. As of 2026-10, we are learning still that His judgment is the gateway to His nearness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
